evidence.intent_output: FR-PROXY-017: a TOTAL_TIMEOUT reached before the response was handed to res.relay must be reported as 504 with kind TOTAL_TIMEOUT through onError. Actual: the client gets 200 followed by an aborted connection, and only the logger sees the failure.

findings.title: A deadline that fires after the head is parsed but before res.relay is reported as an aborted 200, not a 504
findings.description: Between ResponseParser.read and res.relay, the forward path calls ResponseParser.framing, res.status, applyResponseHeaders, the RelayedBodyStream constructor and releaseOnAbort, and it never checks exchange.firedKind(). If the total deadline (or a write deadline that lost its disarm race) fires in that window, the watchdog has already recorded TOTAL_TIMEOUT and closed the plain socket. The proxy still hands the dead body to res.relay. The first read fails, RelayedBodyStream.fail settles TOTAL_TIMEOUT, logs it, and the framework aborts after committing the backend's status. So a timeout that was reached before the relay is reported with the after-relay contract (abort plus log) instead of 504 through the error flow. The window is small in production (it needs a scheduling stall or GC pause), so impact is low. The probe needed an injected delay to make it deterministic.
findings.suggested_fix: Just before res.relay(relayedBody, framing.relayLength), and also right after ResponseParser.read returns, check ProxyException.Kind k = exchange.firedKind(). If it is non-null, throw new ProxyException(k, null). The existing finally then releases the exchange. Add a test that uses a Response wrapper with a delay, as the probe did.

evidence.intent_output: FR-PROXY-017: writeTimeout applies to a backend socket write that makes no progress

findings.drop_reason: The counter-example is confounded. The backend application read every 435 ms or less, but TCP silly-window avoidance only reopens the receive window after about an MSS (16 KiB on loopback) is freed. So the proxy's 8 KiB socket write really made no progress for more than 1 s. That does not prove the write deadline fires on a write that is progressing.
findings.title: A per-write deadline might fire on a write that is slowly making progress
findings.description: The deadline covers the whole 8 KiB write call, not progress inside it. This is only observable when drain progress is below TCP window granularity, which counts as no progress at the sender.

evidence.output: The backend reads 64 KiB, sends 401, calls shutdownOutput and then drains the rest of the body. The proxy's write therefore never fails, and the test does not go through sendRequest's writeFailure or earlyResponse path. It would pass on the pre-diff code.
evidence.intent_output: FR-PROXY-015 AC-6 describes exactly this half-close-and-drain scenario

findings.drop_reason: The test follows the AC text literally. The failed-write early-response path is covered by the two AC-8 tests with an injected write failure (failWritesAfter). This is test design, not a defect.
findings.title: The AC-6 early-401 test does not exercise the failed-write early-response path

evidence.output: Every socket write of up to 8 KiB allocates a WriteDeadline and runs a schedule and a cancel on one JVM-wide ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor queue. A 64 MiB body means about 8192 queue operations under the queue's single lock, shared by all concurrent proxied requests.

findings.drop_reason: Not proven by measurement. No benchmark showed a throughput regression.
findings.title: Per-write schedule and cancel on a global queue
findings.description: Possible contention point under high concurrency.

evidence.output: The watchdog thread is created lazily from a request thread, so it inherits that thread's ThreadGroup, inheritable thread-locals and access-control context. Only the context class loader is cleared.

findings.title: The JVM-wide watchdog thread inherits context from the first request thread
findings.description: Possible temporary class-loader retention in container redeploys.

findings.description: Checked backendFailure, firedKindOr, earlyResponse and BackendClient.open.

clean_code.principle: DRY: the same 'settle own kind, then re-wrap with the fired kind' logic appears in three places
clean_code.description: backendFailure, firedKindOr and RelayedBodyStream.fail each call exchange.settle(own) and build a new ProxyException when the settled kind differs. One ProxyExchange helper, for example ProxyException settled(ProxyException own, Throwable cause), would remove the repetition.
The fallback 'kind != null ? kind : INVALID_RESPONSE' cannot be reached, and its comment says so. A non-null-returning settle overload would remove it.

ProxyExchange now holds resource lifetime (slot, reservation, socket), deadline state, three output-stream decorators (FiredGuard, WatchedOutputStream, WriteDeadline) and the JVM-wide Scheduler executor. Scheduler and the write-deadline stream would fit better in their own types.

The field 'fired' and the method firedKind() also hold kinds the request thread settled itself (READ_TIMEOUT, INVALID_RESPONSE, CONNECT_FAILED). sendRequest's 'firedKind() != null' check depends on settle never running before it. A name such as 'settledKind' would make that invariant visible.
TlsConnector.WATCHDOG and ProxyExchange.Scheduler are separate scheduled executors that both close a plain socket on a deadline. The diff says so, and the move is deferred to wave-19 (REL-PROXY-002).
